claim: Cilia and flagella are model systems for studying how mechanical forces control morphology.
source: Cilia and flagella are model systems for studying how mechanical forces control morphology.
evidence: This is a general statement about the research context presented in the abstract.

claim: The periodic bending motion of cilia and flagella is thought to arise from mechanical feedback.
source: The periodic bending motion of cilia and flagella is thought to arise from mechanical feedback: dynein motors generate sliding forces that bend the flagellum, and bending leads to deformations and stresses, which feed back and regulate the motors.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: Dynein motors generate sliding forces that bend the flagellum.
source: The periodic bending motion of cilia and flagella is thought to arise from mechanical feedback: dynein motors generate sliding forces that bend the flagellum, and bending leads to deformations and stresses, which feed back and regulate the motors.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description of flagellar motion based on established knowledge.

claim: Bending of flagella leads to deformations and stresses, which feed back and regulate the motors.
source: The periodic bending motion of cilia and flagella is thought to arise from mechanical feedback: dynein motors generate sliding forces that bend the flagellum, and bending leads to deformations and stresses, which feed back and regulate the motors.
evidence: This describes the feedback mechanism in flagellar motion.

claim: Three alternative feedback mechanisms have been proposed for flagellar beat regulation: regulation by sliding forces, regulation by curvature, and regulation by normal forces.
source: Three alternative feedback mechanisms have been proposed: regulation by the sliding forces, regulation by the curvature of the flagellum, and regulation by the normal forces that deform the cross-section of the flagellum.
evidence: This statement summarizes existing theoretical proposals in the field.

claim: The curvature control mechanism accords best with the bending waveforms of Chlamydomonas flagella.
source: In this work, we combined theoretical and experimental approaches to show that the curvature control mechanism is the one that accords best with the bending waveforms of Chlamydomonas flagella.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data and theoretical modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: Motors respond to the time derivative of curvature, rather than curvature itself.
source: We make the surprising prediction that the motors respond to the time derivative of curvature, rather than curvature itself, hinting at an adaptation mechanism controlling the flagellar beat.
evidence: This prediction is derived from the theoretical model and fitting to experimental data.

claim: An adaptation mechanism may control the flagellar beat.
source: We make the surprising prediction that the motors respond to the time derivative of curvature, rather than curvature itself, hinting at an adaptation mechanism controlling the flagellar beat.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the finding about time derivative response.

claim: The axoneme contains nine doublet microtubules.
source: The internal motile structure, the axoneme, contains nine doublet microtubules, a central pair of single microtubules, motor proteins of the axonemal dynein family and a large number of additional structural and regulatory proteins (Pazour et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a well-established structural fact about axonemes, supported by citation.

claim: The axoneme contains a central pair of single microtubules.
source: The internal motile structure, the axoneme, contains nine doublet microtubules, a central pair of single microtubules, motor proteins of the axonemal dynein family and a large number of additional structural and regulatory proteins (Pazour et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a well-established structural fact about axonemes, supported by citation.

claim: Axonemal dyneins power the beat by generating sliding forces between adjacent doublets.
source: The axonemal dyneins power the beat by generating sliding forces between adjacent doublets (Summers and Gibbons, 1971; Brokaw, 1989).
evidence: This is a fundamental mechanism of flagellar motion, supported by citations.

claim: Sliding is converted to bending by constraints at the base of the axoneme and/or along the length of the axoneme.
source: The sliding is then converted to bending (Satir, 1965) by constraints at the base of the axoneme (e.g. the basal body) and/or along the length of the axoneme (e.g. nexin links) (Brokaw, 2009).
evidence: This describes the mechanical conversion process, supported by citations.

claim: It is not known how the activities of the dyneins are coordinated in space and time to produce the periodic beating pattern of the axoneme.
source: While the mechanism by which the sliding of a doublet is converted to bending is well established, it is not known how the activities of the dyneins are coordinated in space and time to produce the periodic beating pattern of the axoneme.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Bending the axoneme in one direction requires higher dynein activity on one side of the axoneme than on the other.
source: For example, bending the axoneme in one direction requires higher dynein activity on one side of the axoneme than on the other; if the activities are equal then the forces will cancel and there will be no bending.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the mechanical structure of the axoneme.

claim: The switching of dynein activity is rapid, taking place twice per beat cycle and at rates above 100 times per second for Chlamydomonas.
source: The switching of dynein activity is rapid, taking place twice per beat cycle and at rates above 100 times per second for Chlamydomonas.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation about the dynamics of Chlamydomonas flagella.

claim: The coordination required for rapidly alternating bending is thought to result from mechanical feedback.
source: The coordination required for such rapidly alternating bending is thought to result from mechanical feedback: the axonemal dyneins generate forces that bend and deform the axoneme; and the deformations, in turn, regulate the dyneins.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework for understanding dynein coordination.

claim: In the sliding control mechanism, dyneins behave as 'slip bonds' and detach when subject to forces acting parallel to the long axis of the microtubule doublets that oppose sliding.
source: (i) In the sliding control-mechanism, the dyneins behave as 'slip bonds': they detach when subject to forces acting parallel to the long axis of the microtubule doublets and that oppose sliding (Brokaw, 1975; Jülicher and Prost, 1997; Camalet and Jülicher, 2000; Riedel-Kruse et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes one of the proposed regulatory mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: In the curvature-control mechanism, the detachment of dynein is regulated by doublet curvature.
source: (ii) In the curvature-control mechanism, the detachment of dynein is regulated by doublet curvature (Morita and Shingyoji, 2004; Brokaw, 1972; Brokaw, 2009).
evidence: This describes another proposed regulatory mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: In the normal-force control mechanism (geometric clutch), the detachment of dynein is regulated by transverse forces that act to separate adjacent doublets when they are curved.
source: (iii) In the normal-force control mechanism, also called the geometric clutch, the detachment of dynein is regulated by transverse forces that act to separate adjacent doublets when they are curved (Lindemann, 1994b).
evidence: This describes the third proposed regulatory mechanism, supported by citation.

claim: The two-dimensional model projects the cross-section of the three-dimensional axoneme onto a pair of filaments.
source: In the two dimensional model, we project the cross-section of the three-dimensional axoneme onto a pair of filaments (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the theoretical modeling approach used in the study.

claim: The two filaments in the model have the same polarity with all motors moving towards the base.
source: The two filaments have the same polarity (all motors move towards the base) and have combined bending rigidity κ.
evidence: This is a specification of the theoretical model.

claim: Bending an axoneme into a shape with constant curvature requires the integrated motor force to be independent of arc-length.
source: According to the static force-balance equation, bending an axoneme into a shape with constant curvature requires the integrated motor force to be independent of arc-length, which in turn requires the motor forces be concentrated near the distal end (Mukundan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical inference from the force-balance equation, supported by citation.

claim: The fundamental mode accounts for 90% of the total power in the tangent angle power spectrum.
source: Because the peak at the fundamental frequency (n=1) accounts for 90% of the total power, we neglected the higher harmonics (n = 2,3,4, ...) for reconstructing the flagellar shape.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the Fourier analysis of experimental data.

claim: Using just the n=0 and n=1 modes gave excellent reconstitutions of both the wild type and mbo2 beats.
source: We found that using just the n=0 and n=1 modes gave excellent reconstitutions of both the wild type and mbo2 beats (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is a result from the data analysis, shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The static and fundamental modes provide a good description of the beats.
source: Thus, the static and fundamental modes provide a good description of the beats.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: The time-averaged shape of wild type axonemes is close to a semi-circular arc of radius ≈4 μm.
source: This corresponds to an approximately constant static curvature ≈0.25 rad/μm, and indicates that the time-averaged shape is close to a semi-circular arc of radius ≈4 μm.
evidence: This is derived from the measured static curvature.

claim: mbo2 mutant axonemes have a small static mode, with a curvature ≈0.025 rad/μm, corresponding to an approximately symmetric waveform.
source: In contrast, mbo2 mutant axonemes have a small static mode, with a curvature ≈0.025 rad/μm, corresponding to an approximately symmetric waveform.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Both wild type and mutant axonemes have approximately sinusoidal dynamic beats whose amplitudes dip in the middle of the axoneme and whose wavelengths are approximately equal to their lengths.
source: Thus, both wild type and mutant axonemes have approximately sinusoidal dynamic beats whose amplitudes dip in the middle of the axoneme and whose wavelengths are approximately equal to their lengths.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental observations.

claim: The curvature-control model provided a good fit to the experimental data for both wild type and mbo2 axonemes.
source: The curvature control model provides a good fit to the experimental data for both wild type and mbo2 axonemes (Figure 4A and B, middle panel).
evidence: This is a result from fitting the theoretical model to experimental data, shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The sliding-control model provided a poor fit to the observed beating patterns.
source: The sliding-control model provides a poor fit to the observed beating patterns.
evidence: This is a result from fitting the theoretical model to experimental data.

claim: In the sliding-control model, the real and imaginary parts of the predicted mode are in anti-phase, corresponding to a standing wave and contradicting the observed propagating wave.
source: In the latter case, the real and imaginary parts of the predicted mode are in anti-phase (Figure 4A, left panel), corresponding to a standing wave and contradicting the observed propagating wave.
evidence: This is a result from the theoretical model fitting, shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The normal-force model provided good fits to the experimental data for wild type axonemes.
source: Similar good agreement for wild type axonemes was found with the normal-force model.
evidence: This is a result from fitting the theoretical model to experimental data.

claim: Sliding control cannot produce wave propagation for axonemes as short as those of Chlamydomonas.
source: We argued that the reason for this is that sliding control cannot produce wave propagation for axonemes as short as those of Chlamydomonas (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a theoretical argument supported by model predictions shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The normal-force model relies on the presence of static curvature.
source: While the normal-force model (also termed the geometric clutch model) provided good fits to the experimental data, it relies on the presence of static curvature (Bayly and Wilson, 2015), which varies greatly between the mbo2 and wild type axonemes.
evidence: This is an observation about the requirements of the normal-force model, supported by citation.

claim: The control parameters in the normal-force model had to be varied over a wide range to fit the data from different axonemes.
source: As a result of this large difference in static curvature, the control parameters in this model had to be varied over a wide range to fit the data from the different axonemes (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a result from fitting the normal-force model to experimental data, shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The curvature-control model provided a good fit to the experimental data with similar parameters for mbo2 and wild type axonemes.
source: Finally, the curvature-control model provided a good fit to the experimental data with similar parameters for mbo2 and wild type axonemes.
evidence: This is a result from fitting the curvature-control model to experimental data.

claim: Only the curvature-control model is fully consistent with the experimental data.
source: Thus, we conclude that only the curvature-control model is fully consistent with our experimental data.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on comparing model predictions to experimental data.

claim: The two-dimensional model oversimplifies the normal-force model because it does not distinguish between radial and transverse forces.
source: While this captures the essential features of the sliding control and curvature control models, it oversimplifies the normal-force model, because in the three-dimensional axoneme there are radial and transverse forces acting on the doublets as the axoneme bends. Yet the two-dimensional model does not distinguish between them.
evidence: This is a limitation of the two-dimensional model acknowledged by the authors.

claim: A three-dimensional model shows that even when there is a static curvature (without twist), normal (transverse) forces are not antagonistic across the centerline and therefore cannot serve as a control parameter for motors.
source: The three-dimensional model shows that even when there is a static curvature (without twist), normal (transverse) forces are not antagonistic across the centerline and therefore cannot serve as a control parameter for motors.
evidence: This is a result from a three-dimensional model developed in other work by the authors.

claim: Sliding control can account for the beating patterns of sperm.
source: Earlier results showed that sliding control can account for the beating patterns of sperm (Camalet and Jülicher, 2000; Riedel-Kruse et al., 2007; Brokaw, 1975).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: The bull sperm axoneme is approximately five times longer than the Chlamydomonas axoneme.
source: This is consistent with the present results because the bull sperm axoneme is approximately five times longer than the Chlamydomonas axoneme and we have shown that sliding control can lead to bend propagation in long axonemes (Figure 5 and see Brokaw, 2005).
evidence: This is a comparative observation about axoneme lengths.

claim: Sliding control can lead to bend propagation in long axonemes.
source: This is consistent with the present results because the bull sperm axoneme is approximately five times longer than the Chlamydomonas axoneme and we have shown that sliding control can lead to bend propagation in long axonemes (Figure 5 and see Brokaw, 2005).
evidence: This is a result from the theoretical model, shown in the referenced figure and supported by citation.

claim: Different control mechanisms may operate in different cilia and flagella, with sliding control being used in longer axonemes and curvature control being used in shorter ones.
source: Thus, it is possible that different control mechanisms operate in different cilia and flagella, with sliding control being used in longer axonemes and curvature control being used in shorter ones.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Curvature control models can account for bull sperm data.
source: However we do note that curvature control models can account for the bull sperm data (Riedel-Kruse et al., 2007), as well as data from other sperm (Brokaw, 2002; Brokaw, 1985; Bayly and Wilson, 2015), so there is no strong morphological evidence favoring either sliding or curvature control in sperm.
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings, supported by citations.

claim: The curvature control model robustly describes symmetric and asymmetric beats in short and long axonemes.
source: Thus, the curvature control model, unlike the other two models, robustly describes symmetric and asymmetric beats in short and long axonemes, and could serve as a 'universal' regulator of flagellar mechanics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of different models.

claim: The motor force depends only on the time derivative of the curvature in the curvature control model.
source: An unexpected feature of our curvature control model is that the motor force depends only on the time derivative of the curvature.
evidence: This is a result from fitting the model to experimental data.

claim: Current views of curvature control assume motors respond to instantaneous curvature rather than its time derivative.
source: Such a model is fundamentally different from the current views of curvature control, in which motors are thought to respond to instantaneous curvature (Brokaw, 1972; Brokaw, 2002; Brokaw, 2009) and not to its time derivative.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous theoretical models, supported by citations.

claim: There may be a curvature adaptation system analogous to that of sensory systems, like the signaling pathway of bacterial chemotaxis.
source: One possibility is that there is a curvature adaptation system analogous to that of sensory systems, like the signaling pathway of bacterial chemotaxis (Macnab and Koshland, 1972; Yi et al., 2000; Shimizu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis to explain the time derivative response, supported by citations to analogous systems.

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying curvature sensing are unknown.
source: The molecular mechanisms underlying curvature sensing are unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The strain in a curved microtubule (radius of curvature 4 μm) is very small (≈1%), corresponding to a sub-angstrom strain in a tubulin dimer.
source: A difficulty with dyneins directly sensing microtubule curvature is that the strain in a curved microtubule (radius of curvature 4 μm) is very small (≈1%), corresponding to a sub-angstrom strain in a tubulin dimer.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured curvature.

claim: The dynamic and static components of the beat are regulated independently.
source: Our dynamic curvature control model adds to the view that dynamic and static components of the beat are regulated independently.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results.

claim: The dynamic beats of wild type and mbo2 are similar.
source: Yet the dynamic beats of wild type and mbo2 are similar, as also noted in (Eshel and Brokaw, 1987).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, supported by citation.

claim: Static curvature is 'adapted' away in the dynamic curvature control model.
source: Our dynamic curvature control model provides a solution to this problem because static curvature is 'adapted' away.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the model accounts for the independence of static and dynamic modes.

claim: Power generation (the beat) and steering (the asymmetry) can be independently controlled so that the swimming direction can be adjusted without having to alter the motor properties.
source: This has important biological implications: power generation (the beat) and steering (the asymmetry) can be independently controlled so that the swimming direction can be adjusted without having to alter the motor properties.
evidence: This is a biological interpretation of the model results.

claim: The molecular origin of asymmetry is not known.
source: We note, however, that the molecular origin of asymmetry is not known nor is the mechanism by which the mbo2 mutation leads to symmetric beats (see Geyer et al., 2016 for a discussion of possible mechanisms).
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge, with reference to further discussion.

claim: The mechanism by which the mbo2 mutation leads to symmetric beats is not known.
source: We note, however, that the molecular origin of asymmetry is not known nor is the mechanism by which the mbo2 mutation leads to symmetric beats (see Geyer et al., 2016 for a discussion of possible mechanisms).
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge, with reference to further discussion.

claim: For a traveling wave moving from base to tip, the motor force is nearly out of phase with the sliding displacement and tangent angle.
source: Thus, the exact theory shows that curvature leads the motor force by approximately one quarter of a cycle and is nearly out of phase with the sliding displacement.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model.

claim: The Chlamydomonas flagellum does not operate close to optimal efficiency.
source: Our finding that the motor force is nearly out of phase with the sliding displacement (and tangent angle) shows that the Chlamydomonas flagellum does not operate close to optimal efficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the predicted motor phase to the optimal phase defined by Machin.

claim: The maximally efficient phase for motors is at 225 degrees (compass bearing SW).
source: Machin showed that for a plane wave, the optimum occurs when the phase of the motors is at 225 degrees (compass bearing SW), considerably different from our predicted motor phase, which is <180 degrees.
evidence: This is a result from Machin's theoretical work on optimal efficiency.

claim: Unlike sperm, which Machin calculated to be close to the optimum, the short cilia of Chlamydomonas deviate considerably from optimum efficiency.
source: Thus, unlike sperm, which Machin calculated to be close to the optimum, the short cilia of Chlamydomonas deviate considerably from optimum efficiency.
evidence: This is a comparison between Chlamydomonas and sperm based on theoretical calculations.

claim: The reason that Chlamydomonas deviates from optimum efficiency is that the elastic dissipation dominates over the viscous dissipation.
source: The reason that Chlamydomonas deviates from optimum efficiency is that the elastic dissipation dominates over the viscous dissipation.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the theoretical model.

claim: For an asymmetric beat like that of Chlamydomonas, in which the static and dynamic modes have approximately equal amplitudes, the elastic loss is almost twice as great as that for a symmetric beat.
source: Elastic dissipation arises from the straightening of the bent axoneme and the loss of the associated bending energy (for an asymmetric beat like that of Chlamydomonas, in which the static and dynamic modes have approximately equal amplitudes, the elastic loss is almost twice as great as that for a symmetric beat).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the theoretical model.

claim: The short length of Chlamydomonas axonemes has important implications for the energetics of the flagellar beat.
source: Thus, the short length of Chlamydomonas axonemes has important implications for the energetics of the flagellar beat.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the energetic analysis.

claim: The relatively small viscous dissipation allows us to understand why the curvature mechanism is sensitive to the rate of change of curvature rather than the instantaneous value.
source: The reasoning behind the relatively small viscous dissipation also allows us to understand why the curvature mechanism is sensitive to the rate of change of curvature rather than the instantaneous value.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the theoretical model.

claim: The dynamic curvature dependence is a consequence of the viscous forces being small compared to the elastic forces.
source: Thus, the dynamic curvature dependence is a consequence of the viscous forces being small compared to the elastic forces.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The shortness of the axonemes implied that the sliding control model only generated a standing wave and so could not recapitulate the observed traveling wave.
source: Indeed, it was the shortness of the axonemes that implied that the sliding control model only generated a standing wave and so could not recapitulate the observed traveling wave.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The shortness of the axonemes gave rise to the imaginary curvature control coefficient, leading to the dynamic curvature-control mechanism.
source: Furthermore, it was the shortness that gave rise to the imaginary curvature control coefficient, leading to the dynamic curvature-control mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical analysis.

claim: The shortness of the axonemes implies that the viscous dissipation is small compared to the elastic dissipation.
source: In addition, the shortness implies that the viscous dissipation is small compared to the elastic dissipation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the theoretical analysis.

claim: These conclusions are robust because the power of 1/4 in the expression for the critical length makes it quite insensitive to the parameter values.
source: These conclusions are robust because the power of 1/4 in the expression for the critical length makes it quite insensitive to the parameter values.
evidence: This is an argument for the robustness of the conclusions based on the mathematical form of the critical length.

claim: The long length of sperm leads to quantitatively different properties (e.g the viscous and elastic energies are of similar magnitude, leading to efficient motion, as argued by Machin).
source: The long length of sperm leads to quantitatively different properties (e.g the viscous and elastic energies are of similar magnitude, leading to efficient motion, as argued by Machin).
evidence: This is a comparison with sperm based on the theoretical model and Machin's work.

claim: Whether the long axonemes use the same dynamic curvature-control mechanism as short axonemes will require further study.
source: Whether the long axonemes use the same dynamic curvature-control mechanism as short axonemes will require further study.
evidence: This identifies a question for future research.

claim: Axonemes from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii wild type cells (CC-125 wild type mt+ 137c) were purified and reactivated.
source: Axonemes from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii wild type cells (CC-125 wild type mt+ 137c, R.P. Levine via N.W. Gillham, 1968) and mutant cells that move backwards only (CC-2377 mbo2 mt-, David Luck, Rockefeller University, May 1989) were purified and reactivated.
evidence: This describes the experimental materials and methods.

claim: Mutant cells that move backwards only (CC-2377 mbo2 mt-) were purified and reactivated.
source: Axonemes from Chlamydomonas reinhardtii wild type cells (CC-125 wild type mt+ 137c, R.P. Levine via N.W. Gillham, 1968) and mutant cells that move backwards only (CC-2377 mbo2 mt-, David Luck, Rockefeller University, May 1989) were purified and reactivated.
evidence: This describes the experimental materials and methods.

claim: Trajectories of 20 points along the arc-length of the axoneme were tracked as a function of time over up to 200 beat cycles.
source: We tracked trajectories of 20 points along the arc-length of the axoneme as a function of time over up to 200 beat cycles (Figure 2iii).
evidence: This describes the experimental data collection method.

claim: The uncertainty of the position in xy space was ≈5 nm.
source: The uncertainty of the position in 𝐱𝐲 space was ≈5 nm and the uncertainty in the tangent angle was ≈20 mrad (Figure 2iv-v).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of experimental precision, shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The uncertainty in the tangent angle was ≈20 mrad.
source: The uncertainty of the position in 𝐱𝐲 space was ≈5 nm and the uncertainty in the tangent angle was ≈20 mrad (Figure 2iv-v).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of experimental precision, shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The uncertainty in tangent angle of ≈20 mrad corresponds to a sliding displacement between adjacent doublet microtubules of only 1.3 nm.
source: The latter corresponds to a sliding displacement between adjacent doublet microtubules of only 1.3 nm.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured uncertainty in tangent angle.

claim: Wild type Chlamydomonas axonemes swim counterclockwise in circles at a slow angular rotation speed ωrot≈30 rad/s.
source: Before doing so, we note that wild type Chlamydomonas axonemes swim counterclockwise in circles at a slow angular rotation speed ωrot≈30 rad/s (Figure 2Ai,iii).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The mean localization uncertainty of the center position of each segment was about 5 nm.
source: The mean localization uncertainty of the center position of each of these segments was about 5 nm (Figure 2Aiv and Biv).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of experimental precision, shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The average static curvature for wild type axonemes is C₀=-0.232±0.009 μm⁻¹.
source: The average static curvature is C0=−0.232±0.009 μm−1, the length L=11.7 ± 0.4,μ⁢m, and the frequency ω=427 ± 19 rad/s (68 Hz).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis, reported in Table 1.

claim: The average length of wild type axonemes is L=11.7 ± 0.4 μm.
source: The average static curvature is C0=−0.232±0.009 μm−1, the length L=11.7 ± 0.4,μ⁢m, and the frequency ω=427 ± 19 rad/s (68 Hz).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis, reported in Table 1.

claim: The average frequency of wild type axonemes is ω=427 ± 19 rad/s (68 Hz).
source: The average static curvature is C0=−0.232±0.009 μm−1, the length L=11.7 ± 0.4,μ⁢m, and the frequency ω=427 ± 19 rad/s (68 Hz).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis, reported in Table 1.

claim: The static curvature of mbo2 mutant axonemes was C₀=-0.0276±0.005 μm⁻¹.
source: The static curvature was C0=−0.0276±0.005 μm−1, the length L=9.2±0.3 μm, and the frequency ω=176 ± 44 rad/s, (28 Hz).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis, reported in Table 2.

source: The static curvature was C0=−0.0276±0.005 μm−1, the length L=9.2±0.3 μm, and the frequency ω=176 ± 44 rad/s, (28 Hz).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis, reported in Table 2.

claim: The average frequency of mbo2 mutant axonemes is ω=176 ± 44 rad/s (28 Hz).
source: The static curvature was C0=−0.0276±0.005 μm−1, the length L=9.2±0.3 μm, and the frequency ω=176 ± 44 rad/s, (28 Hz).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data analysis, reported in Table 2.

claim: The basal stiffness in the mbo2 mutant is about 20-fold smaller than in the wild type.
source: A striking difference between the wild type and mbo2 axonemes is that the curve-fitting indicates that the basal stiffness in the mutant is about 20-fold smaller than in the wild type (Table 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a result from comparing the fitted parameters in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The softening at the base in mbo2 is associated with a larger basal sliding in the mutant.
source: This softening at the base is associated with a larger basal sliding in the mutant.
evidence: This is an observation from the fitted parameters.

claim: The coefficient of determination R² for sliding control in wild type axonemes is 49 ± 4%.
source: Coefficient of determination R2(%) 49 ± 4
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of model fit quality, reported in Table 1.

claim: The coefficient of determination R² for sliding control in mbo2 mutant axonemes is 72 ± 5%.
source: Coefficient of determination R2(%) 72 ± 5
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of model fit quality, reported in Table 2.
